newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINLAND SEES LONG-TERM GROWTH, HIGH-TECH KNOW-HOW.
newsitem.headline: FINLAND SEES LONG-TERM GROWTH, HIGH-TECH KNOW-HOW.

text.p: Finland expects to retain its Nordic welfare state far into the future, also with a European single currency, thanks to growth based on a determined focus on high-tech know-how, the government said in a report on Tuesday.
The report to parliament, part two of the coalition's view of Finland's future, said sustained economic growth and reduced unemployment were fundamental objectives.
"The aim is to sustainably reform the welfare systems as successfully as possible within the framework of our own resources," the government said.
Europe was on the brink of economic and monetary union (EMU), which would bring deep change.
"The third stage of EMU is likely to be implemented on schedule in 1999. After that, Europe will not be the same for any country, whether or not it is in EMU among the first," the report said.
The long-term future review did not say whether Finland should join the single currency in the first wave.
Under favourable economic circumstances, social welfare spending as part of gross domestic product would be in decline until population ageing started causing tax pressures around 2010, it said.
By 2035, social spending would rise to over 40 percent of GDP compared to 38 percent at the height of the recession in the early 1990s, and less than 35 percent in 1997, it said.

"In a post-recession situation the foundation for sensible policy is to try to achieve strong, steady growth. Growth will help to survive challenges posed by the public debt, the financing of pensions and unemployment in decades to come."
With 3.5 percent annual average growth, the deficit of the state finances would fall to 0.5 percent of GDP by 2001 from an estimated 4.6 percent this year, the report said.

The forest industry would remain important for Finland but growth would rest ever more on sectors relying on non-material inputs like innovation and skill, not on traditional capital- and energy-intensive refining of raw materials.
Clusters based on know-how were becoming a Finnish specialty, the report said, listing information and communications technology, health care technology and environmental technology applications.
The growth outlook in these areas was better than in other sectors of industry, the report said.

Demand for forest industry products would continue to grow steadily for at least 15 years, with annual worldwide paper demand increasing by two to four percent, and demand for mechanical forest products rising 0.5-2 percent.
"Finland can in the future continue to be successful in the production of such forest industry products where it has or can achieve benefits of economies of scale or through integration," it said.

Cheap energy would be "of essential importance" to refine Finland's extensive spruce raw wood assets into natural fibre-based paper grades, it said, but did not offer any recommendation how to secure sufficient energy.
